executive_summary: Wave and tidal energy remains pre-commercial for Northbridge's stage focus, but two inflection points merit active monitoring: offshore wind co-location economics that could remove wave energy's transmission cost disadvantage, and a go-to-market shift toward behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers that bypasses utility procurement timelines. Recommend monitoring for two quarters while these positioning shifts clarify, with primary risk that neither commercial model gains traction before developer cash runs out. The sector is not investable today, but the strategic repositioning away from grid-scale generation is the first change to the near-term economics case the firm has heard that warrants continued attention.

market_shifts.description: The first U.S. onshore wave energy project launched at the Port of Los Angeles on September 9, 2025, marking commercial entry into the U.S. market where no such deployment existed before.

U.S. federal permitting reform for marine energy advanced through Congress in mid-2026, with legislation specifically targeting streamlined licensing pathways for marine energy devices and removing regulatory barriers for routine maintenance.

Go-to-market strategy is shifting from utility-scale grid power to behind-the-meter offshore industrial applications, with at least one developer pivoting to offshore industrial customers because utility procurement timelines were too slow relative to their burn rate.

Wave energy is being reconsidered as a co-location technology with offshore wind farms to share existing offshore substation and transmission infrastructure, rather than competing as a standalone grid-scale generation source - a potential shift in commercial positioning that could remove one of wave energy's biggest cost disadvantages.

Ireland's ORESS offshore renewable energy support scheme expired by the end of 2025, requiring design of a successor support scheme for tidal and offshore renewables in 2026 with expanded role for the Maritime Area Regulatory Authority.

A major oil company (Shell) completed a wave energy pilot in partnership with Eco Wave Power from 2024 through March 2026 at the Port of Los Angeles, with Eco Wave Power submitting a final project completion report, representing direct corporate engagement from a fossil fuel incumbent in wave energy testing.

new_entrants.name: Eco Wave Power
new_entrants.differentiation: Operates onshore wave energy installations and is publicly traded on Nasdaq (WAVE), with the only deployed wave energy project in the United States and partnership with Shell for commercial pilot testing.

new_entrants.name: CorPower Ocean
new_entrants.differentiation: Selected to lead the €30 million Horizon Europe-backed POWER-Farm project to validate wave farm technology in UK waters, and claims integrating wave energy into hybrid systems reduces installed capacity needs by 20% and lowers LCOE from €81/MWh to €74/MWh.

new_entrants.name: Orbital Marine Power
new_entrants.differentiation: Scotland-based tidal turbine developer advancing international commercial tidal stream projects and expanding its existing turbine fleet.

new_entrants.name: ZOEX Power
new_entrants.differentiation: The UK's only female-founded wave energy company, based in Aberdeen, advancing wave energy converter technology.

tensions_or_conflicts.statement: Northbridge's internal view going into a recent industry summit was that wave energy remained pre-commercial and too early for the firm's stage focus. External evidence from late 2025 through mid-2026 shows the first U.S. commercial wave energy project launched at the Port of Los Angeles in September 2025, Shell completed a multi-year pilot with Eco Wave Power through March 2026, and three European developers secured £7M, £531K, and €30M respectively for commercial-scale advancement and fleet expansion. A reader would have to believe that wave energy has moved from purely R&D to early commercial deployment with corporate and government backing, contradicting the view that it remains too early for venture attention.

Northbridge's internal scouting notes characterize minimal wave energy deal flow (fewer than a handful of intros in the most recent quarter) as consistent with the firm's view that wave/marine energy is one of the least mature sub-segments in advanced energy generation. External evidence shows U.S. federal permitting reform advanced through Congress in mid-2026 with legislation specifically targeting streamlined marine energy licensing, the National Hydropower Association called for tailored licensing pathways to accelerate deployment, and Ireland is designing a successor offshore renewable support scheme for 2026. A reader would have to believe that regulatory infrastructure is being built out to support commercial deployment, which typically precedes rather than follows maturity, suggesting the low deal flow may reflect regulatory bottlenecks clearing rather than fundamental immaturity.

recommendations.text: Monitor wave energy co-location with offshore wind for two quarters to assess whether shared transmission infrastructure economics materialize in bankable project structures, with primary risk that the co-location thesis remains theoretical and no offshore wind developer commits capital to joint deployments. Northbridge's own scouting notes flag offshore co-location as the first argument that meaningfully changes the near-term economics case for wave energy, since it was not part of the firm's original thinking, and an offshore wind developer's business development lead suggested larger players are watching wave energy specifically for this application rather than as competing standalone technology.

Monitor go-to-market pivots toward behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers (oil & gas platforms, offshore aquaculture, ocean sensor networks) for two quarters to see whether developers successfully close contracts and demonstrate revenue, with primary risk that the addressable market for these niche applications proves too small to support venture-scale outcomes. A wave energy founder told Northbridge scouts they shifted from utility offtake to offshore industrial customers because utility procurement timelines were too slow relative to their burn rate, and the firm's scouting notes identified this as a go-to-market pivot worth watching elsewhere in the sub-segment.

Source an intro to the unnamed point-absorber wave energy company pursuing behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers once they are willing to go on record, to understand their customer pipeline depth and unit economics compared to diesel gensets or subsea cables, with primary risk that the company's pivot reflects desperation rather than product-market fit and their industrial pipeline is shallow. Northbridge's own scouting notes recommend this follow-up call, and understanding whether this go-to-market strategy is viable would inform whether to track other developers attempting the same positioning.

Pass on grid-scale wave and tidal energy opportunities for the current fund cycle, because current costs of $0.20/kWh to $0.85/kWh remain 3x to 28x more expensive than mature renewables at $0.03/kWh to $0.12/kWh, and a May 2026 analysis argues the central unsolved commercial challenge for wave energy is ongoing maintenance costs rather than energy conversion itself, with primary risk that Northbridge misses early-mover advantage if maintenance costs drop faster than the reference class forecast suggests. The firm has not run formal diligence on any wave energy company to date, deal flow remains minimal, and wave energy still represents a small fraction of marine renewable discussion compared to offshore wind.

all_claims.claim: Orbital Marine Power (Scotland-based tidal turbine developer) secured a £7 million (approximately €8 million) investment announced December 9, 2025 to advance international commercial tidal stream projects and expand its turbine fleet.

ZOEX Power (Aberdeen-based, described as the UK's only female-founded wave energy company) raised £531,000 (about $715,000-$717,000) in funding announced in late May 2025 to advance its wave energy converter technology.

CorPower Ocean (Swedish wave energy developer) was selected to lead the €30 million Horizon Europe-backed POWER-Farm project, announced around December 9, 2025, aimed at validating wave farm technology in UK waters and addressing competitiveness and bankability of wave farms.
Eco Wave Power (Nasdaq: WAVE) launched the first onshore wave energy project in the United States at the Port of Los Angeles on September 9, 2025, in partnership with Shell and AltaSea.
The Eco Wave Power/Shell Port of Los Angeles pilot was a 100 kW installation that could potentially be expanded into a 60 MW commercial wave energy project at the same port.

Eco Wave Power and Shell entered into a Pilot Test Agreement in 2024 for development, installation, testing and reporting of the onshore wave energy pilot, and Eco Wave Power submitted its final project completion report to Shell around March 31, 2026, successfully concluding the Port of Los Angeles pilot program.
Eco Wave Power's Q3 2025 report described plans for expansion of a Taiwan project to 20 MW in the medium term and potentially up to 400 MW of capacity across Taiwan's coastline.

Eco Wave Power's operating expenses increased 28% to $3.15 million for the relevant reporting period, per an SEC-filed press release, though this figure represented a 24% reduction in operating expenses compared to the third quarter of 2025.

A May 2025 U.S. Marine Energy Cost Performance report (openei.org/MHKDR) found wave and tidal energy costs are currently about $0.20/kWh to $0.85/kWh, compared to roughly $0.03/kWh to $0.12/kWh for more mature renewables per IRENA 2024 figures.

CorPower Ocean states that integrating wave energy into hybrid systems results in a 20% reduction in installed capacity needed and brings levelized cost of energy (LCOE) down from €81/MWh to €74/MWh, with further reductions projected by 2050.

The U.S. National Hydropower Association's 2025 permitting reform factsheet calls for a new, tailored licensing pathway specifically for marine energy technologies to accelerate deployment of marine energy projects nationwide.

The U.S. Senate advanced hydropower legislation (the FLOWS Act and related bills) that includes a targeted licensing measure removing regulatory barriers to speed up routine maintenance and streamlining permitting specifically for marine energy devices, reported roughly mid-2026.

In Ireland, the ORESS (Offshore Renewable Energy Support Scheme) expired by the end of 2025, and a successor support scheme for tidal/offshore renewable energy must be designed by 2026, with a bigger role planned for the Maritime Area Regulatory Authority (MARA).
A market research report published around December 18, 2025 projects the global wave and tidal energy market to reach $1.85 billion by 2032, with commercial-scale deployment anticipated by 2031.

A May 2026 CleanTechnica analysis using reference class forecasting argues that for CorPower Ocean's grid-tested wave technology, the central unsolved commercial challenge is not the wave energy conversion itself but ongoing maintenance costs, implying continued skepticism about near-term commercial viability of wave energy despite technical progress.

Northbridge has not run formal diligence on any wave energy company to date; its informal prior view, going into a recent industry summit, was that wave energy remained pre-commercial and too early for the firm's stage focus.

Wave/marine energy inbound deal flow remains minimal (fewer than a handful of intros in the most recent quarter), which the firm's quarterly sector scan states is consistent with its internal view that wave/marine energy is one of the least mature sub-segments in advanced energy generation.

Wave energy generated more side conversations at a recent industry summit than in prior years, but still represents a small fraction of overall marine/offshore renewable discussion compared to offshore wind.

Northbridge's scouting notes observed that renewed interest in wave energy appears to be coming from a narrower use case than grid-scale power generation - specifically powering offshore infrastructure directly (e.g., oil & gas platforms transitioning to lower-carbon auxiliary power, offshore aquaculture, ocean sensor networks) rather than competing head-to-head with offshore wind for utility-scale generation.

A wave energy founder using a 'point absorber' design told Northbridge scouts they shifted go-to-market from utility offtake to behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers because utility procurement timelines were too slow relative to their burn rate - flagged internally as a go-to-market pivot worth watching elsewhere in the sub-segment.

An offshore wind developer's business development lead suggested to Northbridge that some larger offshore wind players are watching wave energy as a potential co-location technology (sharing existing offshore substation and transmission infrastructure) rather than as a competing standalone technology, which could remove one of wave energy's biggest cost disadvantages if it plays out.

Northbridge's own scouting notes flag the offshore co-location angle as the first argument the firm has heard that meaningfully changes the near-term economics case for wave energy, since it was not part of the firm's original thinking - i.e., this is a potential update to a previously more negative internal view, explicitly noted as such by the firm.

Northbridge's scouting notes recommend a follow-up scouting call with the unnamed point-absorber wave energy company once they are willing to go on record, to better understand their behind-the-meter offshore industrial customer pipeline.
